# must

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/pabloamadorc/must/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/pabloamadorc/must/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

**must** (*MUltiple STressors*) detects and classifies non-additive effects of
multiple stressors in experiments. It makes explicit the three decisions
behind any claim of synergism or antagonism:

1. **What the design can identify.** `describe_design()` reports missing
   treatment combinations, cells shared by several contrasts, the
   replication unit, stressors applied to whole groups of units (blocks,
   whole plots, rooms) and repeated measures, and which interactions are
   identifiable, before any model is fitted.
2. **Which model fits the data.** `fit_responses()` fits a generalised linear
   mixed model (glmmTMB) to each response and chooses its error distribution
   by convergence, simulation-based residual checks (DHARMa) and AIC.
3. **What "non-additive" means.** `estimate_interactions()` tests the simple
   addition (AD), multiplicative (MU) and dominance (DO) null models from the
   predictions of that single model (post-estimation inference, Madge
   Pimentel et al. 2025), by default with a correction for experiments with
   few replicates. With three or more stressors it separates the net
   deviation from the single-stressor effects from the pure highest-order
   interaction. `classify_interactions()` gives the directional classes of
   Piggott et al. (2015).

Orr et al. (2020) name the use of null models as a major unresolved issue in
multiple-stressor research and ask researchers to know the alternatives and
how each relates to a statistical test; must is built to report them side by
side.

> **Status:** version 0.1.0, not yet on CRAN. The interface may still
> change.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("pabloamadorc/must")
# The residual checks used to choose each model need DHARMa:
install.packages("DHARMa")
```

## Example

`polazzo_zooplankton` holds the zooplankton of a mesocosm experiment with a
full factorial of an insecticide, a herbicide and nutrients, three mesocosms
per combination, sampled four times after the pesticide application
(Polazzo & Rico 2021, CC0).

```{r design}
library(must)
zoo <- polazzo_zooplankton[polazzo_zooplankton$day > 0, ]

design <- describe_design(
  zoo,
  stressors = c("insecticide", "herbicide", "nutrients"),
  control = c(insecticide = "absent", herbicide = "absent", nutrients = "ambient"),
  unit = "mesocosm",
  time = "day"
)
design
```

One model per response. `residual_checks = TRUE` (the default) uses DHARMa;
it is switched off here only so that this example runs without it.

```{r fit}
fits <- fit_responses(zoo, c("total_density", "cyclopoida", "daphnia"), design,
                      residual_checks = FALSE, seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
fits
```

Interactions under the three null models, with Krinsky–Robb intervals and
the small-sample correction (the default):

```{r estimate}
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, n_sim = 4000, seed = 2021)
summary(est)
```

The three-stressor set on day 7, with and without the correction
(`correction = "none"` is the asymptotic procedure of Madge Pimentel et al.
2025):

```{r day7}
asymptotic <- estimate_interactions(fits, n_sim = 4000, seed = 2021, correction = "none")
day7 <- function(x) {
  e <- x$estimates
  e <- e[e$response == "total_density" & e$time == "7" & e$order == 3L &
           e$component == "interaction" & e$null_model == "AD",
         c("estimand", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "df", "p_value", "p_adjusted")]
  e[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")] <- lapply(e[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")], signif, 3)
  e[c("p_value", "p_adjusted")] <- lapply(e[c("p_value", "p_adjusted")], signif, 2)
  e
}
day7(est)
day7(asymptotic)
```

On day 7 the three-stressor combination falls below the sum of the single
effects (`net`), but its pure third-order interaction does not differ from
zero: the net deviation comes mainly from the pairwise interactions (net =
pure + the three pairwise interactions), so it is not, by itself, evidence
of a three-way interaction. With 24 mesocosms in 8 treatment combinations
the correction uses a t distribution with 16 degrees of freedom: the
intervals widen and, once adjusted across the sets and sampling times, the
net deviation is no longer significant, whereas the asymptotic procedure
would call it significant. (The estimates differ slightly because, with
random effects, the corrected ones come from the REML refit.)

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(est, response = "total_density", null_model = "MU", time = c("7", "overall"))
```

```{r classify}
cls <- classify_interactions(est)
table(cls$response, cls$class, useNA = "ifany")
```

"AD" means that no deviation was detected, not that additivity was shown.
`NA` classes are the dominance model, which Table 1 of Piggott et al. (2015)
does not cover, and the sets that need a treatment combination where the
herbicide alone eliminated *Daphnia*: that single effect is tested from the
probability of observing only zeros (`status = "boundary"`), but the
interactions that use it cannot be measured.

## Methods and decisions

| Null model | "No interaction" means | Interaction estimate (two stressors) |
|---|---|---|
| AD, simple addition | changes add up on the response scale | yAB − yA − yB + y0 |
| MU, multiplicative | relative changes multiply | ln yAB − ln yA − ln yB + ln y0 |
| DO, dominance | the strongest single effect prevails | min(yAB, y0) − min(yA, yB) |

* **Estimands.** For k ≥ 3 stressors, `net` = yK − Σ yi + (k − 1) y0 (or on
  the log scale) and `pure` = inclusion–exclusion over all 2^k combinations.
  DO is defined for two stressors only. By default, interactions are
  estimated with the other stressors at control; `background = "all"` in
  `describe_design()` also estimates them in the presence of the others.
* **Inference.** Krinsky–Robb simulation (as in Madge Pimentel et al. 2025)
  or the delta method for AD and MU. By default (`correction =
  "small_sample"`) the covariance comes from a REML refit and the sampling
  distribution is a t with the degrees of freedom of the experimental units
  (column `df`); `correction = "none"` reproduces the asymptotic procedure.
  p-values are adjusted with Benjamini–Hochberg across contrast sets and
  sampling times; averages over times (`time = "overall"`) are adjusted
  separately, and pre-treatment samplings declared in `baseline` are not
  tested.
* **Responses.** Counts, continuous values with or without zeros (Tweedie),
  successes out of a number of trials (`trials`) and counts per unit of
  effort (`offset`); one dispersion for all, per `by` group or per
  treatment combination (`dispersion`). A combination with only zeros is
  tested from the probability of that outcome under the null model.
* **Assumptions.** Means are conditional on random effects at zero; MU and
  DO assume that an increase in the response means tolerance (declare the
  responses where it means sensitivity in `sensitivity`); a random intercept
  per unit does not model temporal autocorrelation (an AR1 structure can be
  given in `random`); selection of the error distribution is not included in
  the uncertainty.

`vignette("must")` walks through these decisions in more detail.

## Status of the checks

* Verified against independent results: cell means and delta-method
  standard errors for Gaussian and Poisson models (hand calculations); with
  the small-sample correction, the AD intervals of a Gaussian model equal
  those of `lm()`; Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom with one
  dispersion per combination; the probability of a combination with only
  zeros (closed forms and numerical integration); the dominance estimate;
  the identity *net = pure + pairwise interactions* for three stressors;
  and the 45 rows of Table 1 of Piggott et al. (2015).
* Type I error and power in simulated 2 × 2 experiments (Gaussian, Gamma,
  negative binomial and Poisson models, with and without repeated
  measures). With three replicates per combination, the asymptotic tests
  rejected a true null model in 10–17% of the experiments (Gaussian AD
  12.8%, Gamma MU 13.5%, negative binomial MU 10.3%, Gaussian DO 16.5%) and
  the corrected ones in 2–7%; Poisson tests, without a dispersion
  parameter, are the same either way.
* Tried on seventeen published multiple-stressor data sets with different
  designs (full and partial factorials with two to twelve stressors,
  gradients, blocks, split plots, repeated measures, pre-treatment
  samplings, survival out of a number of animals, counts per unit of effort,
  sequential exposures): the description of each design matches an
  independent tabulation of the original files, and the results that do not
  depend on the model (raw cell means, net deviations as sums of pure
  interactions) agree; 90 checks, all passed.
* `R CMD check` runs on Linux, macOS and Windows with GitHub Actions,
  including the DHARMa residual checks.
